name: New Zealand
tagline: A genuinely dramatic pair of islands where fjords, glaciers, geothermal fields and volcanic alpine crossings sit within a few hours' drive of each other.
cardDescription: Milford Sound's cliffs, Rotorua's geothermal fields, Queenstown's adventure sports, and a living Maori culture found nowhere else on Earth.
metaDescription: A complete New Zealand travel guide: the 10 best places to visit, driving, Maori culture, food, costs and a practical two-week South and North Island itinerary.

image.file: File:Milford Sound in Fiordland National Park 01.jpg
image.alt: Mitre Peak rising above the still waters of Milford Sound

intro: New Zealand packs a genuinely improbable range of landscapes into two main islands roughly the size of the United Kingdom — glaciers descending almost to rainforest, geothermal fields that steam and bubble beside working towns, fjords carved by ice into vertical cliffs, and volcanic alpine crossings that feel like walking on another planet.

That geological drama is inseparable from a living Maori culture with a genuinely unbroken presence stretching back centuries before European arrival — Te Reo Maori place names cover the map, and a hangi feast or haka performance is a real cultural encounter, not a staged tourist show, in the places that do it properly.

The country divides cleanly into two islands with distinct characters: the North Island holds most of the population, the geothermal fields and Maori cultural centres, while the South Island holds the more dramatic mountain, fjord and glacier scenery that dominates New Zealand's international image. A well-organised road network and domestic flights make combining both islands in one trip genuinely straightforward, though the distances involved reward building in more driving time than the map alone suggests.
placesIntro: Ordered roughly by how strongly we would recommend each for a first visit — though Abel Tasman and the Bay of Islands reward a second trip just as much as a first.
thingsToDoIntro: The experiences that recur across the country and that make a New Zealand trip feel like more than a checklist of dramatic landscapes.

thingsToDo.title: See a Maori cultural performance
thingsToDo.text: A genuine haka performance and cultural evening, particularly around Rotorua, offers real insight into Maori history and tradition rather than a staged photo opportunity.
thingsToDo.tip: Seek out a marae-based or iwi-run cultural experience over a generic hotel dinner show for a genuinely more authentic encounter.

thingsToDo.title: Try an adventure sport

image.alt: The Kawarau Gorge Bridge near Queenstown, birthplace of commercial bungee jumping

thingsToDo.text: Queenstown genuinely invented commercial bungee jumping at the Kawarau Gorge Bridge in 1988, and the wider region remains the world's most concentrated hub for skydiving, jet boating and canyon swings.
thingsToDo.tip: Book adventure activities a few days ahead in peak summer — the most popular operators genuinely sell out.

thingsToDo.title: Hike the Tongariro Alpine Crossing

image.file: File:Volcanic features in Tongariro Alpine Crossing.jpg
image.alt: Volcanic craters and coloured lakes along the Tongariro Alpine Crossing

thingsToDo.text: Widely considered one of the world's best day hikes, the crossing genuinely traverses active volcanic terrain, emerald crater lakes and stark alpine desert in a single demanding day.
thingsToDo.tip: Check current volcanic activity alerts before setting out, and book a shuttle in advance since the trail is one-way.

thingsToDo.title: Soak in Rotorua's geothermal springs

image.alt: Steaming geothermal hot springs near Rotorua

thingsToDo.text: Rotorua's genuinely active geothermal field means natural hot pools, bubbling mud and sulphur-scented steam rising from parks and streets throughout the town.
thingsToDo.tip: A dedicated thermal spa offers a more comfortable soak than the free public pools, which can run uncomfortably hot.

thingsToDo.title: Spot New Zealand's iconic wildlife

image.file: File:22 Kiwi warning sign in New Zealand - kiwi bird wildlife warning sign.jpg
image.alt: A yellow kiwi crossing warning sign, an iconic sight on New Zealand roads

thingsToDo.text: The nocturnal, flightless kiwi is genuinely New Zealand's national symbol, rarely seen in the wild but reliably spotted at dedicated conservation centres, alongside fur seals, dolphins and whales around the coast.
thingsToDo.tip: A guided nocturnal kiwi encounter at a conservation centre is genuinely the most reliable way to see one — wild sightings are rare.

thingsToDo.title: Visit Hobbiton

image.alt: The hobbit holes of the Hobbiton movie set near Matamata

thingsToDo.text: The genuine, permanently maintained film set from The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit trilogies, its hobbit holes and gardens tended year-round rather than left as a temporary prop.
thingsToDo.tip: Book tickets online ahead — access is by guided tour only and popular time slots genuinely sell out.

foodIntro: New Zealand food draws on genuinely excellent local produce, Maori tradition and a strong café culture found at every price point.

foods.name: Hangi

image.alt: A traditional Maori hangi, food cooking in an earth oven

foods.text: A traditional Maori method of cooking meat and vegetables in a pit oven heated by hot stones, genuinely producing a distinctive smoky, tender result found at cultural experiences nationwide.
foods.whereToTry: Maori cultural centres, particularly around Rotorua, offering a genuine hangi feast as part of an evening experience.

foods.name: Pavlova

image.alt: A pavlova dessert topped with cream and fresh fruit

foods.text: A meringue-based dessert with a genuinely crisp shell and marshmallow-soft centre, topped with whipped cream and fresh fruit — a beloved national dessert, its exact origin still debated with Australia.
foods.whereToTry: Cafés and home kitchens nationwide, especially at Christmas and summer gatherings.

foods.name: Fish and chips

image.alt: A classic New Zealand fish and chips takeaway

foods.text: A genuinely beloved national tradition, usually made with fresh local snapper or tarakihi, eaten straight from the paper on a beach or waterfront.
foods.whereToTry: Independent fish and chip shops nationwide, especially good near any coastal town.

foods.name: Meat pie

image.file: File:Steak and cheese pie - Napier, New Zealand.jpg
image.alt: A classic New Zealand steak and cheese meat pie

foods.text: A genuinely serious national obsession — flaky pastry filled with steak, mince or a range of other fillings, sold at every bakery and petrol station nationwide.
foods.whereToTry: Independent bakeries nationwide; a good pie is a genuine point of local pride in every town.

foods.name: Green-lipped mussels

image.alt: Green-lipped mussels, a New Zealand seafood specialty

foods.text: A genuinely distinctive New Zealand species, farmed extensively in the Marlborough Sounds and served simply steamed or in a range of sauces.
foods.whereToTry: Seafood restaurants nationwide, especially good fresh in Picton and the Marlborough region.

foods.name: Hokey pokey ice cream

image.alt: Hokey pokey, a New Zealand ice cream flavour with honeycomb toffee pieces

foods.text: Vanilla ice cream studded with pieces of honeycomb toffee, genuinely one of New Zealand's most distinctive and beloved local ice cream flavours.
foods.whereToTry: Ice cream parlours and supermarkets nationwide — a genuine Kiwi childhood staple.

practicalIntro: The essentials, current for 2026. New Zealand is straightforward and well organised to travel in, with genuinely long driving distances and changeable weather the two practicalities that most often catch visitors out.

practical.language: English and Te Reo Maori, both official languages, with English used in almost all visitor contexts.
practical.money: Card payment is widely accepted nationwide, including contactless for small purchases, though carrying some cash is worthwhile in smaller rural towns.
practical.visa: Most visitors need an NZeTA (New Zealand Electronic Travel Authority) applied for online before arrival, even for visa-waiver countries — apply at least 72 hours ahead.
practical.plugs: Type I (the same three-pin type used in Australia), 230 V, 50 Hz.
practical.tipping: Not expected or customary. Restaurant prices already reflect fair wages, and tipping can genuinely seem confusing to service staff.
practical.safety: Very safe overall, consistently ranked among the world's safest countries. The greater real risk is from nature — changeable weather, strong currents and remote hiking terrain — rather than crime.
practical.connectivity: Good 4G coverage in towns and cities, thinning out considerably in remote and mountainous areas — a local SIM covers most visitor needs.
practical.timeZone: New Zealand Standard Time (UTC+12), New Zealand Daylight Time (UTC+13) from late September to early April — among the first countries in the world to see each new day.

budget.label: Backpacker
budget.value: NZ$100–150 per day — hostels, casual meals, buses

budget.label: Mid-range
budget.value: NZ$220–350 per day — 3-star hotels, restaurant dinners, a rental car

budget.label: Comfortable
budget.value: NZ$450–700+ per day — boutique lodges, fine dining, guided tours

bestTime.headline: December–February for summer, or shoulder seasons for fewer crowds
bestTime.summary: New Zealand's seasons run opposite the Northern Hemisphere's, and the specific window matters more here than in most destinations because of how weather-dependent many activities are.

seasons.text: The warmest, driest weather and the longest days, ideal for hiking, beaches and the Great Walks — also the busiest and most expensive season.
Mild, settled weather with genuinely spectacular autumn colour in Central Otago, and noticeably thinner crowds than summer.
Cold, especially in the South Island, but genuinely excellent for skiing around Queenstown and Wanaka, with the North Island staying milder.
Increasingly mild with lambing season in full swing, though mountain weather remains genuinely unpredictable this early in the season.

bestTime.avoid: Book Great Walks huts, Milford Sound cruises and Queenstown accommodation many months ahead for the December–February peak — this is genuinely the busiest and most tightly booked window of the year.

tripDuration.headline: 14–21 days to cover both islands properly
tripDuration.summary: New Zealand's genuinely long driving distances mean a rushed itinerary does the country a disservice — this is not a place to try to see everything in a week.

options.text: One island only — either the North Island's cities and geothermal fields, or the South Island's mountains and fjords.
options.detail: Trying to cover both islands in under 10 days genuinely means too much time driving and not enough time anywhere.

options.text: A South Island loop covering Christchurch, Queenstown, Milford Sound and the West Coast glaciers, the most popular single-island itinerary.
options.detail: Add a few days in Wanaka or Abel Tasman if the pace allows.

options.text: The itinerary on this page: Auckland, Rotorua, Wellington across the North Island, then Christchurch, Queenstown, Milford Sound and the glaciers across the South.
options.detail: A domestic flight between the islands, rather than the ferry, saves genuinely significant time on a trip this length.

options.text: Add the Bay of Islands, Tongariro and Abel Tasman in full, all genuinely worth dedicated time rather than a rushed add-on.
options.detail: A longer trip is where New Zealand's driving distances stop feeling like a constraint and start feeling like the point.

transport.intro: New Zealand rewards a rental car more than almost any other destination in this guide — public transport between towns is genuinely limited.

options.text: Genuinely the standard way to see New Zealand — distances between [[queenstown|Queenstown]], [[milford-sound|Milford Sound]] and the [[franz-josef-glacier|glaciers]] are far longer than they look on a map.
options.detail: Book well ahead in summer, and budget considerably more driving time than a map suggests for winding mountain roads.

options.text: Connect [[auckland|Auckland]], [[wellington|Wellington]], [[christchurch|Christchurch]] and [[queenstown|Queenstown]] quickly, genuinely worth it for a trip covering both islands in under three weeks.
options.detail: Book ahead for the best fares — routes between the main hubs run frequently.

options.text: Connects [[wellington|Wellington]] to Picton across Cook Strait, a genuinely scenic crossing through the Marlborough Sounds.
options.detail: Book vehicle space well ahead in summer — sailings can sell out.

options.text: InterCity coaches connect most towns nationwide, a workable budget option for visitors without a car.
options.detail: Considerably slower than driving, but a genuinely functional way to see the country on a tighter budget.

options.text: Multi-day coach tours cover the country's highlights without needing to drive yourself.
options.detail: A genuinely good option for visitors uncomfortable with unfamiliar mountain roads or long driving days.

culture.intro: New Zealand culture is shaped by a genuine, living Maori heritage alongside a relaxed, outdoorsy national character, with a handful of broadly shared norms holding nationwide.

etiquette.title: Maori culture deserves genuine respect
etiquette.text: Learning a few Te Reo Maori words, and approaching cultural experiences like a hangi or marae visit with real openness, is genuinely appreciated.

etiquette.title: A relaxed, first-name culture is the norm
etiquette.text: New Zealanders are genuinely informal and friendly by nature — a casual, direct manner is standard rather than a sign of rudeness.

etiquette.title: Take mountain and coastal safety seriously
etiquette.text: Weather genuinely changes fast in alpine and coastal areas — check forecasts and conditions before any hike or water activity.

etiquette.title: Tipping isn't expected
etiquette.text: Restaurant and service prices already reflect fair wages — leaving a tip is genuinely unusual rather than customary.

etiquette.title: Respect biosecurity rules
etiquette.text: New Zealand's border controls on food, plants and outdoor equipment are genuinely strict — declare everything and clean hiking boots before arrival.

etiquette.title: BYO and shared plates are common dining customs
etiquette.text: Many restaurants genuinely allow you to bring your own wine (BYO) for a small corkage fee — worth asking about.

dos: Learn a few Te Reo Maori words and place names — genuinely appreciated as a sign of respect.
Book Great Walk huts, Milford Sound cruises and Queenstown accommodation well ahead in the summer peak.
Check mountain and coastal weather forecasts before any hike or water activity — conditions genuinely change fast.
Declare all food, plants and used outdoor gear at the border — biosecurity checks are genuinely strict.
donts: Don't summit Ngauruhoe or Tongariro out of respect for their sacred status to Ngati Tuwharetoa, even where technically allowed.
Don't expect to tip at restaurants or cafes — it's genuinely unusual rather than customary.
Don't underestimate South Island driving times — winding mountain roads genuinely take longer than a map suggests.
Don't skip travel insurance with hiking and adventure-sport cover — conditions and activities here carry genuine real risk.

tipsIntro: Practical notes on booking, timing and driving that make a real difference to a New Zealand trip.
tips: Apply for an NZeTA online at least 72 hours before arrival — most visitors need one, even from visa-waiver countries.
Book a rental car well ahead in summer, and budget more driving time than a map alone suggests for mountain roads.
Book Great Walks huts, Milford Sound cruises and Hobbiton tickets online well ahead in peak season.
Check mountain and coastal weather forecasts before any hike — conditions genuinely change fast.
Declare all food, plants and outdoor equipment at the border — biosecurity rules are genuinely strict.
Consider a domestic flight between islands rather than driving the full length, if time is limited.

faq.q: How many days do you need in New Zealand?
faq.a: Two weeks covers one island properly. Eighteen days to three weeks allows the fuller North-and-South itinerary in this guide, with time for the Great Walks, glaciers and fiords without constant rushing.

faq.q: Do you need a car in New Zealand?
faq.a: Genuinely, yes, for most itineraries. Public transport between towns is limited, and a rental car gives the flexibility needed to reach Milford Sound, the glaciers and smaller towns on your own schedule.

faq.q: Is New Zealand expensive to visit?
faq.a: Moderately to considerably expensive by global standards, comparable to Australia, with accommodation and rental cars the biggest costs. Camping, hostels and cooking your own food bring costs down significantly.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit New Zealand?
faq.a: December to February (summer) offers the most reliable weather for hiking and the Great Walks, though it's also the busiest and most expensive. March to May offers a genuinely excellent shoulder-season alternative with thinner crowds.

faq.q: Should I visit the North Island or South Island?
faq.a: The South Island holds the more dramatic mountain, fjord and glacier scenery that dominates New Zealand's international image; the North Island holds most of the population, the geothermal fields and the strongest Maori cultural experiences. A first trip of two weeks or more genuinely benefits from covering both.

faq.q: Do I need a visa for New Zealand?
faq.a: Most visitors need an NZeTA (New Zealand Electronic Travel Authority), applied for online before arrival, even from countries with visa-free access — apply at least 72 hours ahead of your flight.
